paras: The Boston Spur ambush killing was the killing of an unnamed 16-year-old Black boy, shot from ambush at Boston Spur, in east Grant parish, Louisiana, on the afternoon of Wednesday, August 15, 1900. The Alexandria Town Talk and the Colfax Chronicle both condemned the killing, and the Chronicle presented it as part of a wave of threats and shootings aimed at driving Black sawmill workers out of the area.

According to the Colfax Chronicle, there had been "a good deal of high handed violence" in east Grant of late, in which Black men employed at some of the sawmills were threatened, shot at and run off. The Town Talk described the section as one where "some of the white people will not allow a colored person to reside."
At 3 p.m. on August 15, a "colored boy, 16 years old," was "ambushed and shot to death" at Boston Spur. Neither paper named him, gave any accusation against him, or identified his killer or killers.

Ten days later the Chronicle wrote that it did not know what parish officials had done toward locating "the guilty party or parties," and it called on them to take "thorough and vigorous action." It also urged "the good citizens of east Grant" to band together to run down the "cut-throat murderers" behind the outrages there. No report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage.

The killing is known from a single editorial in the Colfax Chronicle of August 25, 1900, headed "Dastardly Murder, the Outcome of Foolish Prejudice," which opened by quoting the Alexandria Town Talk. The Town Talk called the shooting "a cowardly deed" and wanted its author punished, yet added that there was "no need of killing" Black people who came to the section, since a notice to leave would send them away "at double quick time."

The Chronicle went further, calling the running off of Black workers "criminal folly" and closing with a plea to stop "cowardly, brutal murdering" by "a few hoodlums and unworthy vagabonds." Its case rested largely on economics: Black laborers, it argued, did the heavy work white men shunned and so made more skilled jobs for white men in the mills.

reader.title: Boston Spur ambush killing
bases: The Town Talk ties the ambush killing to a section where 'some of the white people will not allow a colored person to reside,' and the Chronicle sets it among threats, shootings and the running off of Black sawmill workers in east Grant by unknown 'cut-throat murderers' (A1, A2).
The only report is one Colfax Chronicle editorial (A1, with its closing lines in A2) that quotes the Alexandria Town Talk; the Town Talk original and any other report were not found.

accounts.label: Alexandria Town Talk (as quoted)
accounts.gist: A 16-year-old colored boy was ambushed and shot to death at Boston Spur in a section where some white people would not allow a colored person to reside; the paper called it cowardly and wanted the author punished.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle editorial
accounts.gist: The killing took place in Grant parish amid recent threatening, shooting and running off of Black sawmill workers in east Grant; the paper urged officials and citizens to catch the 'cut-throat murderers.'

framing.detail: The Alexandria Town Talk called the killing 'a cowardly deed' but wrote that there was 'no need of killing' Black people who came to the section, since a notice to leave would send them away.

Under the headline 'Dastardly Murder, the Outcome of Foolish Prejudice,' the Colfax Chronicle condemned the killing and the running off of Black mill hands, arguing chiefly that Black labor did work white men shunned and aided local industry.
